name: Russia
card_headline: Russia and Ukraine resumed US-mediated talks in November, but Putin rejects negotiations after bridge strikes while the economy stalls and repression tightens at home
card_summary: US, Russian and Ukrainian officials met in Abu Dhabi in November for the first time in nine months and agreed a prisoner exchange, but made no breakthrough. [1] Putin then said there would be no negotiations after Ukraine struck the Crimea bridge. [2] Mediazona has named about 289,000 Russian dead. [3] The IMF puts 2026 growth at 0.9 percent. [4] United Russia took 349 Duma seats, though independent analysts put its real vote near 34 to 35 percent. [5][6] Memorial counts 1,680 political prisoners. [7]
card_local: Mediazona has named about 289,000 Russian soldiers killed, and Meduza reports a Kremlin-linked strategist saying the Duma turnout was secured through "very dirty means". [3][8]
card_international: Reuters and Al Jazeera report US envoys meeting Putin in Moscow, a Putin, Trump and Xi summit in Shenzhen on 19 November, and what Russian defence ministry data suggest was the largest overnight Ukrainian drone attack on Russia since 2022. [9][1][10]
card_scholar: Carnegie's Alexandra Prokopenko describes a ruling elite of managers with access to Putin but little influence, and CSIS estimates up to 450,000 Russians dead since the war began. [11][12]
context_md: Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine on 24 February 2022. [13] The war is now close to five years old. [1] Russia annexed four Ukrainian regions in 2022 that it has never fully captured. [1] Political repression has widened through new criminal articles, with Memorial counting 12 added since 2022. [14] Growth was 1 percent in 2025, against more than 4 percent in 2023 and 2024. [15] The State Duma held its first election since the invasion on 18 to 20 September 2026. [5] Putin faces an International Criminal Court arrest warrant. [16]

sections.title: Talks resumed in November, then Putin ruled out negotiations after the bridge strikes
sections.body_md:
Two days of trilateral talks in Abu Dhabi ended on 11 November without a breakthrough. They were the first direct US-mediated talks between Russia and Ukraine in nine months, and they produced a prisoner exchange plan. The US side said some progress was made on post-war security guarantees. [1] On 12 November the US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff met Putin in Moscow. The Kremlin called the talks useful, and Putin rejected any European troop presence in Ukraine and called the front the "line of control". [1] Kyiv rejects Putin's demand that it give up all of Donbas, and the US says differences on territory remain. [1]

On 16 November Ukraine held online talks with Witkoff, Kushner and European representatives. Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov said Russia had not agreed to widen the talks beyond the existing delegations. [9] Putin and Trump met at the APEC summit in Shenzhen on 19 November, and Xi Jinping joined for a trilateral session. Reuters reported beforehand, citing Russian news agencies, that no full-scale bilateral negotiations were planned. [10] Al Jazeera reports that the three issued a "peace declaration" and that the Kremlin said Ukraine was not the central topic of the trilateral meeting. [16]

After Ukraine struck the Crimea bridge again, Putin said there would be no negotiations and that Russia would not accept ceasefires covering energy or the Black Sea, according to The National. [2] German Chancellor Friedrich Merz called the bridge attack a sign of Russian weakness, and European leaders agreed that national security advisers from six capitals and the EU would speak for Europe if talks expand. [2] TASS, a state agency, recorded Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov saying in December 2025 that Moscow's opposition to Western troops in Ukraine is longstanding. [17]

lenses.local: Local sourcing on the November talks is thin in this draft; no exiled Russian outlet piece on them was read.
lenses.international: Reuters, AP and Al Jazeera carry the Abu Dhabi round, the Moscow meeting and the Shenzhen summit. [1][10][16]
lenses.scholar: ISW assessed on 14 November that US proposals for Ukrainian NATO membership implicitly reject Russian demands to halt NATO expansion, and that a requested local ceasefire near Kostyantynivka would help Russia reinforce its southern flank. [18]

sections.title: The front moves slowly while the named Russian dead pass 289,000
sections.body_md:
Mediazona had confirmed the names of about 289,000 Russian dead as of 23 November 2026. Working from Rosstat and probate-registry data, it estimates the true total at more than 700,000, and it says the named list is not exhaustive. [3] CSIS puts Russian dead at up to 450,000 and injured at 1.4 million, a different estimate by a different method, reported through Fortune. [12] No official Russian total appears in the sources read for this draft.

On the ground, ISW assessed on 14 November that Russia was concentrating on the Kostyantynivka and Dobropillya area. Moscow has claimed Kostyantynivka since July, and ISW says Russian forces have not seized it. [18] ISW also reported small Russian gains near Lyman and Slovyansk and Ukrainian counterattacks near Kharkiv and Orikhiv. [18] CSIS says Russian forces advanced as slowly as 50 to 90 metres a day in 2026. [12] ACLED recorded more than 26,500 battle events in Ukraine in the first eleven months of 2025, an all-time high. [19]

Recruitment is falling. The economist Janis Kluge estimates that 71,200 new contract soldiers received enlistment bonuses in the first quarter of 2026, the lowest for that period in three years, against 89,600 a year earlier. [20] Dmitry Medvedev claimed 127,000 new contract soldiers since the start of 2026, a figure Novaya Gazeta Europe says conflicts with budget data. [20] Russia reportedly signed 450,000 recruits in 2024 and 422,000 in 2025. [21]

Ukraine's strikes inside Russia continue. On 14 November the Ukrainian General Staff confirmed a strike on the Samara station that mixes oil for the Urals blend, which ISW says is over half of Russian oil exports. [18]

lenses.local: Mediazona's named list is the main independent count of Russian military dead. [3]
lenses.international: Al Jazeera and Reuters report that Russian defence ministry data indicated the largest overnight drone attack on Russia since 2022 on 16 November. [9]
lenses.scholar: ISW, CSIS and ACLED describe slow Russian gains at high cost, with ACLED counting an all-time high of battle events. [18][12][19]

sections.title: The economy: 0.9 percent growth, a deficit ahead of plan and a key rate of 14 percent
sections.body_md:
The IMF cut its forecast for Russian growth to 0.9 percent for both 2026 and 2027 on 13 October, down from 1.1 percent in its July projection. [4] Meduza reported in May that first-quarter GDP fell 0.3 percent year on year by the Economic Development Ministry's estimate. [15]

The federal deficit for January to August reached 5.8 trillion rubles, 2.5 percent of GDP, against a full-year target of 3.8 trillion, according to a preliminary Finance Ministry estimate reported by Meduza. Oil and gas revenue in the period was 5 trillion rubles, down 16.7 percent. [22] The ministry cited advance payments on state contracts, and Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said the deficit is no cause for serious concern. [22] Three bond auctions were canceled in June and July after yields rose above 16 percent. [22]

The Bank of Russia held its key rate at 14 percent on 11 September, ending ten straight cuts that began in June 2025, and forecast 2026 inflation of 6 to 7 percent. [23] The Bell reported in February that the defence industry accounted for all manufacturing growth since 2022, so civilian industry shrank. [13] It also reported that courts ordered 11.03 billion dollars in assets transferred to the state in 2025, about triple the 2024 figure. [13]

Sanctions and strikes add pressure. The EU's latest listings cover 49 Russian financial institutions and 15 companies tied to the shadow tanker fleet, according to Ukrainska Pravda. [24] ACLED said repeated Ukrainian attacks on refineries reduced Russian refinery output by 20 percent in 2025. [19]

lenses.local: Meduza and The Bell describe a stalling civilian economy and a deficit running ahead of plan. [22][13]
lenses.international: Ukrainska Pravda reports the EU adding 113 listings, including 47 commercial banks. [24]
lenses.scholar: Carnegie's Alexandra Prokopenko calls the economy stuck in a "negative equilibrium", and CSIS says wartime spending may be increasingly untenable. [25][12]

sections.title: A record Duma majority: 349 seats officially, a 34 to 35 percent vote by independent estimate
sections.body_md:
Voting ran from 18 to 20 September 2026. The Central Election Commission reported turnout of 59.8 percent, and United Russia won 349 of 450 seats. The Communists took 37, LDPR 23, New People 19 and A Just Russia 17. [5] Forty-six war participants won seats, 41 of them for United Russia. [5] Officials gave United Russia about 58 percent of the party-list vote. [6]

Independent analysts dispute those figures. Novaya Gazeta Europe and Important Stories, using Sergey Shpilkin's statistical method, estimate United Russia's real share at about 34 to 35 percent and turnout at about 40 percent. [6] Leonid Volkov argues the method fails when no clear core of honest polling stations remains, and remote electronic voting was left out of the analysis because it cannot be verified. [6] A Just Russia cleared the 5 percent threshold only after 97.5 percent of precincts were processed. [6]

Meduza's Andrei Pertsev reports that a deputy governor was told to deliver turnout of 50 percent plus a decent margin, and that sources describe managers assigning staff to track whether employees voted. [8] A strategist working with the Presidential Administration told Meduza the turnout record was secured through very dirty means. [8] These accounts come from unnamed sources and one outlet.

lenses.local: Meduza and Novaya Gazeta Europe supply both the insider accounts and the statistical estimates. [8][6]
lenses.scholar: Carnegie's Alexandra Prokopenko writes that the Duma rubber-stamps executive decisions. [11]

sections.title: Political repression: 1,680 recognised prisoners, 4,800 by a wider count, sentences near 11 years
sections.body_md:
The Memorial Political Prisoners project recognised 1,680 political prisoners as of 30 June 2026, up 93 in one quarter, and counted 5,567 people deprived of liberty in politically motivated cases. [7] OVD-Info puts the number imprisoned or prosecuted for political crimes at no fewer than 4,800, counting only cases it can verify independently. UN Special Rapporteur Mariana Katzarova has called for the release of more than 2,000 political prisoners. [14] The totals differ by organisation, and this draft reports each figure with its owner.

Memorial reported on 17 June that the average sentence for people convicted in 2026 is 11 years, against 6 years and 7 months in 2021. It counted 12 new criminal articles and 12 revised ones that have widened politically motivated prosecution since 2022. [14]

Interior Ministry data reviewed by Mozhem Obyasnit show cases for justifying terrorism rose 28 percent, from 352 to 451, in the first quarter of 2026 against a year earlier. Cases for public incitement to extremism rose 31 percent. [26] The lawyer Ivan Pavlov said most prosecutions under these statutes are political and tied to the war. [26] Memorial's second-quarter barometer counts 513 new prosecutions in Russia itself in the quarter, with about 68 percent of those prosecuted deprived of liberty. [7]

lenses.local: Novaya Gazeta Europe reports the sentence data and the Interior Ministry figures. [14][26]
lenses.scholar: Memorial's quarterly barometer is the main systematic dataset on politically motivated cases. [7]

sections.title: The internet is being closed from inside: shutdowns, throttled messengers and a state app
sections.body_md:
Mediazona's Alexander Borodikhin reports that mass mobile shutdowns are now routine, with mobile internet in central Moscow out for nearly three weeks in March 2026. Authorities cite the threat of Ukrainian drones, but outages have also hit regions far from the front. [27] In February 2026 the State Duma approved a bill that lets the FSB demand that operators cut cellular service. [27] The Bell counted 2,129 regional internet shutdowns in August 2025 alone, more than the whole world recorded in 2024. [13]

Roskomnadzor began blocking voice calls on Telegram and WhatsApp in August 2025, throttled WhatsApp nationwide in late November 2025 and announced tighter Telegram restrictions on 10 February 2026. [27] The state messenger Max, built on VK's platform, was promoted by presidential decree in June 2025. A March 2026 analysis found the Android app probing blocked domains and reporting whether a VPN was active, which Max's press service denied. [27] Al Jazeera's Niko Vorobyov reported in March that Kommersant estimated Moscow's losses at 3 to 5 billion rubles over five days of shutdown, and that Levada found more than one-third of Russians use VPNs. [28]

CPJ counted 27 journalists jailed on criminal charges since the February 2022 invasion: 15 Russian, 10 Ukrainian and 2 American. It also counted 355 journalists and outlets designated foreign agents and 27 outlets banned as undesirable. [29]

lenses.local: Mediazona documents the shutdown, VPN and messenger measures with dates. [27]
lenses.international: Al Jazeera reports that outages reached Moscow and St Petersburg in March 2026 and that observers see a possible test of a whitelist of approved services. [28]
lenses.scholar: CPJ's February 2026 tally is the main systematic count of jailed and designated journalists. [29]

sections.title: Society: 67 percent back peace talks, fertility keeps falling and recruitment strains regions
sections.body_md:
The Levada Center, an independent Moscow pollster, surveyed 1,625 people in 50 regions on 18 to 25 February 2026. Sixty-seven percent backed peace talks, a record, and 24 percent supported continuing the full-scale invasion, the lowest since February 2022. [30] The same poll found 72 percent support the military's actions in Ukraine and 82 percent approve of Putin. [30]

Rosstat data reported by Novaya Gazeta Europe put the 2025 national total fertility rate at 1.361 and the rural rate at 1.464, the lowest rural figure since Soviet times. [31] Carnegie's Alexandra Prokopenko projects unemployment near 2.5 percent for 2026 and argues that low unemployment and repression limit the chance of broad social pressure, though discontent over prices is growing. [25]

Kluge finds that combined federal, regional, municipal and corporate enlistment bonuses cost about 0.5 percent of GDP. Regional budget deficits totalled 1.5 trillion rubles last year, and recruitment takes 3 to 4 percent of regional budgets on average and about 10 percent in Mari El. [21]

lenses.local: Novaya Gazeta Europe and Meduza report the fertility and recruitment-cost data. [31][21]
lenses.international: Bloomberg News carries the Levada poll. [30]
lenses.scholar: Carnegie's Prokopenko links low unemployment and repression to limited social pressure. [25]

scores.coverage_basis: Reuters, AP and Al Jazeera filed on Russia and the war in every week of November, covering the Abu Dhabi talks, the Moscow meeting and the Shenzhen summit. [1][10][16] Exiled outlets Meduza, Mediazona and Novaya Gazeta Europe publish in English at high volume, and Carnegie, CSIS and ISW keep up steady research. [3][14][11][12][18]

severity.basis: Russia is a party to the largest war in Europe in decades, with ACLED recording an all-time high of battle events in 2025 and Mediazona naming about 289,000 Russian dead. [19][3] Ukrainian drones have hit refineries and an air base inside Russia. [18]
Inside Russia the sources read show limited acute need: unemployment is projected near 2.5 percent, though regional budgets are strained by recruitment costs. [25][21]
Memorial recognises 1,680 political prisoners, CPJ counts 355 journalists and outlets as foreign agents, and independent analysts estimate United Russia's real vote at 34 to 35 percent. [7][29][6]
The IMF forecasts 0.9 percent growth, the key rate is 14 percent, and the January to August deficit was 2.5 percent of GDP. [4][23][22]
Sentences have lengthened to 11 years and mobile shutdowns are routine, while growth forecasts fell, though talks resumed in November. [14][27][4][1]

parts.basis: Russia is a nuclear power at war with Ukraine, negotiating with US envoys, and a party to a three-way summit with the US and China on 19 November. [1][16]
ISW says the Urals blend mixed at Samara makes up over half of Russian oil exports, and The Bell reports the ruble and yuan now carry 86 percent of export payments. [18][13]
ACLED counted at least 100 unauthorised drone overflights near sensitive sites across Europe in 2025, and Putin calls European troops in Ukraine legitimate targets. [19][1]
ACLED counted more than 2,000 civilians killed by Russian indiscriminate targeting in Ukraine between January and November 2025. [19]
Russia annexed four Ukrainian regions it does not fully control, Putin faces an ICC arrest warrant, and the Shenzhen declaration criticises the court. [1][16]

summary: Russia scores near the top because it is a nuclear-armed state at war with its neighbour, in direct talks with Washington and in a trilateral format with Beijing. [1][16] Its oil exports, payment shift to rubles and yuan, and drone overflights in Europe tie the war to markets and to NATO states. [18][13][19]
The score is held below the maximum on economic reach because the sources read give Russia's share of world trade only indirectly. [13]
gi.up: A collapse of the talks followed by strikes on NATO territory or Black Sea shipping would raise it.
gi.down: A ceasefire that holds along the line of contact, with verifiable security guarantees, would lower it.

gaps: Local sourcing is almost entirely exiled outlets (Meduza, Mediazona, Novaya Gazeta Europe, The Bell); no outlet reporting from inside Russia was read, and no Russian-language page was opened.
OVD-Info's own reports were not opened; its 4,800 figure and the UN Rapporteur's call come second-hand through Novaya Gazeta Europe.
Chatham House and Crisis Group pieces on Russia were not read; the Chatham House page failed to load and no Crisis Group page was found.
The CSIS casualty and economy findings were read through Fortune, not the CSIS report.
No RIA or RT page was read; TASS appears once, flagged state_affiliated, only for a Kremlin position dated December 2025.
The outcome of the 19 November Putin and Trump bilateral meeting was not located; only the trilateral declaration and the pre-meeting Reuters report were read.
The EU sanctions article gives no adoption date or package number, and the UN civilian casualty figures for 2026 could not be fetched.
Moscow Times pages on Rosneft and Lukoil sanctions showed conflicting dates and were not used; the effect of US oil sanctions on exports is not sourced.
Rosstat and Mediazona totals rest on leaked or estimated data; Medvedev's recruitment claim and Kluge's estimate are not reconciled.
Migration, the North Caucasus, the Russian Far East, religion, Navalny's death and the fate of exiled opposition leaders are not covered in this draft.
Podcast and film links point to listing pages, and the Naked Pravda link goes to the written Q&A, not the audio.
